opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a common picture that if you want to work on AI safety or AI more broadly, the path is to become a researcher: get a PhD, come up with novel ideas, publish papers. And research matters a lot. But in my experience, a huge fraction of the actual progress at the frontier is bottlenecked on engineering, not on ideas.

When you're training large models, the hard part often isn't knowing what experiment to run. People usually have more ideas than they can test. The hard part is building the infrastructure to run that experiment at scale, reliably, and quickly enough that you can iterate. That means distributed systems, getting good efficiency out of thousands of accelerators, debugging weird numerical issues, and building tooling so a researcher can go from idea to result in a day instead of a month. Someone who's great at that can multiply the output of a whole team of researchers.

This applies to safety work too. A lot of the most useful safety research, like interpretability, evaluations, or alignment techniques for large models, requires working with frontier-scale systems. If you can't run things at scale, you can't study the systems that actually matter. So strong engineers are directly enabling safety research, not just capabilities.

There's also a practical career angle. Standard advice can make it sound like you need a research pedigree to contribute, and that discourages many people with strong software backgrounds who could be extremely valuable. Engineering skills are also learnable on the job and transferable. If you've been a good software engineer somewhere else, you can often ramp up on ML engineering faster than you'd expect.

The line between research and engineering is also pretty blurry in practice. Many of the best researchers I know are excellent engineers, and many important "research" insights came from someone carefully building something and noticing that it didn't behave as expected. So I'd encourage people not to see engineering as the lesser path. In many cases it's where the leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says the research–engineering boundary is blurry, notes that strong researchers are also excellent engineers, and describes engineering as directly enabling safety research.

r002.rationale: It says career advice can discourage engineers and frames engineering as wrongly seen as the lesser path, but does not state that engineering has historically received less prestige than research.

r003.rationale: It describes engineering as a major bottleneck and the hard part of running experiments, but does not clearly say engineering accounts for most of the work involved in experimentation.

r004.rationale: The response does not explain that inadequate tooling causes researchers to avoid otherwise worthwhile research directions.

r005.rationale: It says tooling helps researchers move from an idea to a result faster, but does not say that creating tools can open a research direction for other researchers to pursue.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the standard advice people hear is something like: if you want to work on AI, you should go get a PhD, become a research scientist, and spend your time coming up with novel ideas. And I think that's actually pretty mismatched with what the work looks like day to day at a frontier lab.

The honest picture is that most of what we do is engineering. Even the research is engineering. If you look at what actually moves the needle on a big training run, it's things like: can you get the model to train stably at scale, can you make the data pipeline fast enough, can you debug why throughput dropped by 15% on a particular cluster, can you write an evaluation that actually measures what you care about. Those are engineering problems. The "idea" part is often a small fraction of the time, and the ideas that matter tend to be fairly simple. The hard part is executing them at scale without everything falling over.

So when I'm interviewing people, I'm much more excited about someone who can write really solid code, who can take a fuzzy problem and turn it into a working system, who can debug something nobody's seen before, than I am about someone with a long publication list but who struggles to get things running. And I think a lot of people underrate themselves because they think "I'm just a software engineer, I'm not a researcher," when actually that skill set is the bottleneck.

The other thing I'd say is that engineering is a much more legible path in. You can go build things, contribute to open source, get good at distributed systems or performance work, and that's a credential that transfers. Whereas "I have research taste" is really hard to demonstrate from the outside, and honestly a lot of research taste comes from having built enough things that you have intuitions about what will work. So I'd tell most people: if you're deciding between spending two years getting better at engineering versus two years trying to produce novel research, the engineering path is probably the better bet, both for getting hired and for actually being useful once you're there.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes engineering and says research work is largely engineering, but it does not clearly state that AI work requires both research and engineering skills.

r002.rationale: It contrasts common career advice with engineering’s practical value, but does not say engineering has historically received less prestige than research.

r003.rationale: It says most work at a frontier lab is engineering, including research and the work that moves training runs forward.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that poor tooling can lead researchers to avoid worthwhile research directions.

r005.rationale: It does not explain how tools that ease experimentation can enable other researchers to pursue a direction.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of advice about AI careers focuses on coming up with new research ideas, and underweights the engineering work that lets you actually test those ideas. You can have a promising hypothesis, but if you can’t implement it reliably, run the experiment, and understand why it failed, it’s hard to make progress.

And those aren’t cleanly separate activities. When you’re building something, you discover things that change your research direction. Maybe the experiment wasn’t measuring what you thought it was measuring, or an apparent improvement was actually a bug. Having good engineering judgment helps you distinguish those cases.

So I’d encourage people to get experience taking projects all the way through: build something, make it work, evaluate it, and get other people to use it. That gives you useful skills across a range of roles, and it also helps you become a better researcher if that’s where you end up.

r001.rationale: The response presents engineering as helpful to research, but does not clearly state that AI work requires both skill sets or that it is not exclusive to one role.

r002.rationale: It says career advice underweights engineering, but makes no claim about engineering’s historical prestige relative to research.

r003.rationale: It describes engineering tasks involved in testing ideas, but does not state that engineering makes up most AI experimentation work.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that poor tooling can deter researchers from worthwhile directions.

r005.rationale: It does not describe tools that ease experimentation enabling other researchers to pursue a direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of careers advice puts too much emphasis on having ideas and too little on being able to make those ideas work. In AI, the gap between an interesting proposal and a useful result can be a huge amount of engineering: getting experiments running, figuring out why they failed, making the system reliable, and building tools that let other people move faster.

That also makes engineering a useful foundation if you’re uncertain about what you ultimately want to do. You can contribute to research, work on safety, or build products, and you get fairly concrete feedback about whether you’re making progress. Research and engineering aren’t really separate tracks in the way people sometimes imagine. Often, being able to implement something well is what lets you discover whether the research idea was any good.

So I wouldn’t say everyone should become an engineer. But I would encourage people to spend more time building things, and to take that skill seriously as a way of having an impact.

r001.rationale: The response says research and engineering are not separate tracks and that good implementation helps determine whether a research idea works, communicating that AI work draws on both.

r002.rationale: It does not say engineering has historically received less prestige than research.

r003.rationale: It describes engineering as a substantial part of turning proposals into results, but does not say it accounts for most experimentation work.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that poor tooling can lead researchers to avoid worthwhile directions.

r005.rationale: It says tools can help others move faster, but does not state that easier experimentation opens a research direction for others to pursue.
